headline: Speaker Johnson steps aside as House GOP leader.
summary: Mike Johnson won't run for House minority leader in the new Congress, two people familiar with his decision told the AP. Democrats swept the House on Tuesday, so the speaker's gavel passes to them. Republicans pick a new leader next week, likely Steve Scalise or Jim Jordan. Johnson won his Louisiana seat for an eighth term.
cover_answer: No. His team lost, so he gave up being captain.
table_question: If your team lost big, should the captain step down or stay on?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Mike Johnson is the Speaker, the person in charge of the House, where a lot of our laws get made. His team lost the big vote on Tuesday, so he says he won't be the boss of his team anymore. It's like a captain handing over the armband after a hard loss. He still has his job, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A captain handing over the armband is a change they can picture. At six they take your tone as the verdict, so keep it level.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them a captain handing over the armband after a loss, one picture for a shuffle of jobs. They also read your face before your words, and a level voice tells them this is ordinary. Expect "is he sad?" Probably, and he still has a job. Then on.

8-12.script: The party with the most House seats picks the Speaker. Republicans lost that majority on Tuesday, so in January the gavel goes to the Democrats, likely Hakeem Jeffries. Johnson could have run to lead the smaller Republican side; he told his staff he won't. Lose enough games and the captaincy gets rechosen.
8-12.why: One chain: the majority picks the Speaker, the majority flipped, and the leader stepped back. Fair is their subject at eight.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether grown-ups apply them, so the script hands them the rule first: the majority picks the Speaker. Then the chain: the majority flipped, the gavel moves, and Johnson chose not to run for the smaller job. Expect "did he have to quit?" No, he chose to; let them judge the choice.

13-17.script: In October Johnson told CBS he'd stay on whatever happened. After the loss he told staff he won't run. Can a leader change his mind when the numbers change, or was October a campaign line? Second: Axios says Republicans are watching whether Trump backs a successor. Should he get a say?
13-17.why: Two true things: he said he'd stay, and the loss changed the math. At fifteen they can hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: Johnson said in October he would stay on, and after the loss he stepped back. The script asks whether that is a broken promise or a sane reading of new numbers, then whether Trump should pick the successor. Expect "would you have quit?" Answer straight; they are testing you.

5-7.a: No. His team lost, so he gave up being captain. He still works there.

8-12.q: Why can't he be Speaker anymore?
8-12.a: The House majority picks the Speaker. Democrats won it, so they pick.
Republicans vote next week, likely Steve Scalise or Jim Jordan.

13-17.q: Didn't he say he'd stay no matter what?
13-17.a: Yes, to CBS in October. After the loss he told staff he won't run.

13-17.q: Does Trump get to pick the next leader?
13-17.a: Not officially. Republicans vote by secret ballot. He may back someone.
